BATTERY PLANNING

How to Choose Electric Truck Battery Capacity: 166 to 600 kWh

Capacity is a specification, not a range promise. Select a pack only after mapping the work shift, charging window, operating reserve and approved vehicle build.

TCO & CHARGINGSeptember 29, 20269 min read
In this guideCatalogue capacitiesCapacity vs rangeMeasure the duty cycleSize the packTrade-offsCharging integrationChecklistFAQ

Real catalogue capacities span several truck families

The project product data lists different battery choices across tractors, cargo trucks, dump trucks and special vehicles. These are not interchangeable packs and do not imply identical range. The table below is a family-level index to help buyers ask the right model-specific questions. It is not an availability promise or a statement that every capacity can be ordered on every model.

Vehicle family / examplesCatalogue-listed capacitiesImportant boundary
TE electric tractors400 / 466 / 497 / 600 kWh by modelVerify variant, GCW class, pack and connector
KT5M / KT5J 18 t cargo262 / 310 kWhBody, wheelbase and auxiliary demand matter

For example, the TE family includes several heavy tractor classes; a KTA1 entry is listed at 352 kWh; and some urban cargo configurations list 262 or 310 kWh. A capacity comparison without model, axle layout, body and duty cycle can be misleading. Ask for the precise catalogue row and order code that applies to the intended vehicle.

Nominal capacity, usable energy and route range are different

Battery capacity is usually expressed in kilowatt-hours. It describes stored energy under a defined rating, but does not by itself tell a fleet how much energy should be consumed on a routine shift. The manufacturer may specify an operating SOC window, reserve, temperature limits and charging policy. Follow the vehicle-specific documentation; do not assume the entire nominal pack is available for dispatch planning.

Range is an outcome of the energy available and the vehicle's energy use over a route. Energy use changes with mass, speed, acceleration, gradients, road surface, traffic, temperature, tyres, driver behavior and cab or body auxiliaries. A refrigerated body, hydraulic equipment, mixer or refuse system may draw energy independently of the traction motor. That is why a larger pack cannot be translated into a universal number of kilometres.

For procurement, keep three items separate: nameplate capacity, expected shift energy under defined conditions, and reserve for contingencies. If a supplier quotes a range, ask which payload, route, speed, weather, SOC window and auxiliary load were used. Compare claims only when the underlying assumptions are aligned and documented.

Measure the duty cycle before selecting a size

Start with dispatch records. Capture loaded, partially loaded and empty distance, payload or combination mass, elevation, average and peak speeds, stop count, idle and queue time, operating hours and shift changes. Record the body equipment used, cab climate settings, ambient temperature and any unusually difficult segment. For regional fleets, separate route types rather than averaging a short urban delivery and a long highway run together.

Where possible, collect data over representative weeks and include the demanding but normal day. A pilot vehicle or comparable electric truck can produce a more useful energy estimate than converting a diesel route into an assumed electric range. Record SOC at start and end, grid energy delivered, charging session timing, route conditions and payload. Note whether a measurement includes charging losses or only the pack's reported use.

When no measured data exists, make the uncertainty explicit. Create low, expected and demanding cases and label all assumptions. Do not present an illustrative case as actual customer performance or a guaranteed range. A quotation should include a route-specific validation plan before fleet scale-up.

A practical capacity-sizing method

First estimate traction and auxiliary energy required for the planned shift from measured data or a validated engineering estimate. Second, apply the approved SOC window and the operating reserve required by the fleet. Third, compare that requirement with the specific model's approved capacity options and the charging time available before the next dispatch. Finally, verify the vehicle's loaded mass, axle limits, body fit, connector and local approval for that pack.

A simple planning relationship is: energy needed for the shift plus reserve must fit within the usable energy allowed by the vehicle's operating policy. This is a framework, not a calculation result; the supplier's usable-energy guidance and measured operation must provide the real inputs. The battery should also support the fleet's charging pattern. If an overnight window is fixed and charger capacity is constrained, pack size and dispatch schedule need to be evaluated together.

Run sensitivity checks. What happens if a route adds a detour, ambient temperature changes, payload increases, a charger is unavailable or the truck returns later than planned? If the largest listed pack is still insufficient for a route with no reliable charging, selecting it does not solve the operational issue. The route, shift, infrastructure or vehicle class may need to change.

Balance capacity against vehicle, cost and utilization

A larger battery may increase energy buffer, but it can also affect vehicle mass, purchase price, charging demand and the amount of payload available under a legal mass limit. The actual effect depends on the vehicle's engineering and market configuration; request the pack-specific curb mass and approved axle data. Don't assume that two battery choices maintain identical payload or dimensional details.

Consider utilization. If a truck returns to base frequently and can charge in a predictable break, a smaller approved pack may be sufficient for the operation, but this must be validated against measured energy and reserve. Conversely, a longer route with restricted charging may justify a larger pack if it stays within weight, cost and infrastructure constraints. Neither direction is universal. Fleet dispatch discipline and charger availability can change the effective value of battery capacity.

Compare total system cost using the same duty cycle: vehicle and body, charger and site works, electricity tariff, demand charges where applicable, maintenance assumptions, operating days and downtime. See the electric truck TCO calculation guide for a transparent way to expose assumptions. Do not assume a savings percentage or a payback period without fleet-specific inputs.

Make the charging window part of the battery decision

List when each vehicle is available to charge: overnight parking, loading dwell, scheduled breaks or return-to-depot intervals. Identify which windows are guaranteed and which depend on queues. Then ask the charger provider and vehicle supplier to confirm the connector, charging curve, power acceptance, current limits and environmental conditions for the exact configuration. A battery capacity and a maximum current figure do not establish a fixed charging time.

Map simultaneous vehicles and site demand. A fleet that plugs in all units at the same time may have a different infrastructure requirement from one with staggered returns. Include parking layout, cable reach, electrical supply and charger outage plans. Use qualified professionals for site electrical design. For the separate charging workflow, read the 600 kWh tractor depot charging guide; it does not replace a model- and site-specific assessment.

Battery selection checklist for a quote

  • Exact model, body, axle layout, market version and available battery options.
  • Pack-specific vehicle mass, axle loads and approved payload or combination limits.
  • Route distance, loaded mass, grade, speed, stops, weather and auxiliary use.
  • Measured shift energy, measurement conditions and SOC operating guidance.
  • Required operating reserve, detour scenarios and expected annual utilization.
  • Charging connector, curve, limits, available dwell and site electrical capacity.
  • Purchase and infrastructure cost assumptions, tariff and maintenance scope.
  • Pilot success criteria, data collection method and escalation plan.

For product-specific comparison, visit the tractor, cargo and dump truck configuration pages. To receive a matched recommendation, send your route, payload, shift and charging information.

Frequently asked questions

Does 600 kWh mean a truck can travel farther than a 400 kWh truck?

It represents a higher nominal capacity, but real range depends on the vehicle, route, operating mass, usable SOC and energy consumption. Compare model-specific data and measured conditions.

Should I choose the largest available pack for safety?

Not automatically. Check mass, payload, price, charger capacity and the route's measured energy requirement alongside reserve.

Are battery options the same for tractor, cargo and dump trucks?

No. The catalogue lists different capacities by model family. Confirm the chosen model and configuration in writing.
